title: [Inductor] Triton convolution template produces incorrect results for non-1x1 kernels
body_excerpt: The Triton convolution template in TorchInductor produces incorrect results for convolutions with kernel sizes larger than 1x1. This is due to a known Triton loop unrolling issue (triton-lang/triton#1254). ## Error `test_convolution1` in `test/inductor/test_select_algorithm.py` fails with: AssertionError: Incorrect result from choice TritonTemplateCaller( BLOCK_K=16, BLOCK_M=1024, BLOCK_N=16, GROUPS=1, KERNEL_H=3, KERNEL_W=3, PADDING_H=4, PADDING_W=5, STRIDE_H=2, STRIDE_W=3, UNROLL=False ) Mismatched elements: 19584 / 23120 (84.7%) Greatest absolute difference: 132.32015991210938 at index (0, 22, 4, 13) ## To Reproduce python test/inductor/test_select_algorithm.py TestSelectAlgorithm.test_convolution1 Root Cause The Triton conv template (torch/_inductor/kernel/conv.py) uses UNROLL=is_ones(kernel_shape), meaning non-1x1 kernels use a non-unrolled loop pattern. This triggers incorrect results due to triton-lang/triton#1254. cc @ezyang @gchanan @kadeng @msaroufim @chauhang @penguinwu @voznesenskym @EikanWang @jgong5 @Guobing-Chen @XiaobingSuper @zhuhaozhe @blzheng @wenzhe-nrv @jiayisunx @ipiszy @muchulee8 @amjames @aakhundov @coconutruben @jataylo

body_excerpt: I was testing things on my Strix Halo GPU and noticed some NaN/Inf in the result. I tracked it down to wrong results from LayerNorm/RMSNorm. It's caused by these 2 problems: ### 1. Hardcoded warp size In `aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/layer_norm_kernel.cu`, `LaunchGammaBetaBackwardCUDAKernel()` has block_dim_x hardcoded https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/8eae40c58fc6016823374479779646557fb2ac7c/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/layer_norm_kernel.cu#L965-L969 This assume all AMD GPUs use 64 threads per warp (or "wavefront" in AMD's terminology). title: [inductor][static launcher] Missing runtime dtype validation for pointer-typed Triton args can silently produce incorrect results
body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug I believe there is a missing runtime validation in the static Triton launcher path for pointer-typed Triton kernel arguments. I reproduced this on a pip-installed `torch==2.8.0` environment (not running from a source checkout). In that version, the relevant file on the executed code path is: - `torch/_inductor/runtime/static_cuda_launcher.py` I also inspected current `main`, where this code has been renamed to `torch/_inductor/runtime/static_triton_launcher.py`, and I did not find an equivalent runtime validation for pointer-typed tensor dtypes there either. ## Summary The static launcher appears to compress all pointer-typed Triton arguments to `"O"` and does not preserve or validate the original pointer element dtype (for example `*fp16`, `*bf16`, `*fp32`) before launch. This means a kernel compiled assuming one pointer dtype can still be launched at runtime with a tensor of a different dtype, without a clear validation error. body_excerpt: Not sure if this can be classified as a bug but I thought I would post this just incase it isn't known about. body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug When the input tensor contains `NaN` values, the CPU implementation of `torch.linalg.slogdet` propagates that and returns `NaN` as the `logabsdet`. title: `jax.jit` produces NaN/Inf from softmax when pre-activation values are very large; eager returns finite output
body_excerpt: ### Description The model proceeds in five stages: | Step | Operation | Approximate max magnitude | |------|-----------|--------------------------| | 1 | `exp(clip(x, max=4))` over shape `(6,14,14)` | 54.6 per element | | 2 | `sum(axis=0)` — reduce batch of 6 | ~328 | | 3 | `matmul(a, a)` | ~1.5 × 10⁶ | | 4 | `matmul(a, prev)` | ~6.9 × 10⁹ | | 5 | `einsum('ij,jk->ik', c, cᵀ)` (self outer-product) | ~6.7 × 10²⁰ | These values feed into an SDPA block: `softmax(Q @ Kᵀ × scale, axis=-1)`. The pre-softmax scores can reach ~2.5 × 10²¹ — still within float32 range. Numerically stable softmax (`exp(x − max(x)) / Σ exp(x − max(x))`) should handle this correctly. Eager mode does; JIT does not. **Possible root cause:** XLA's compiled softmax (or an XLA fusion of the preceding matmul and softmax) does not correctly apply the max-subtraction stabilization when pre-softmax values are very large (~10²¹). title: Choose rounding mode when casting to dtype
github_labels: module: cuda|triaged|module: type promotion|function request|oncall: pt2|module: inductor|module: floatx (formerly float8)|bot-triaged
body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch `tensor.to(dtype)` performs a round-nearest conversion. This makes sense in most cases, but there are situations where other rounding modes are useful. For example in MXFP8 (microscaled float8) on Blackwell GPUs, we need to convert the scales to their next power of 2 and convert them to a float8_e8m0fnu (i.e., a biased uint8). This could be done in one shot via `scales.to(torch.float8_e8m0fnu, round="up")`. Which then would allow PyTorch to match this exactly to the optimized PTX instruction `cvt.rp.satfinite.ue8m0x2.f32` (`.rp` means round-positive). ### Alternatives Several less-readable alternatives, which will also make it harder for PyTorch and Inductor to understand the intent and thus optimize the code. For example one could go through torch.log and torch.ceil, or through torch.frexp, or do the cast with round-nearest and the conditionally adjust the result. ### Additional context _No response_ cc @ptrblck @msaroufim @eqy @jerryzh168 @tinglvv @nWEIdia @nairbv @mruberry @voznesenskym @penguinwu @EikanWang @jgong5 @Guobing-Chen @XiaobingSuper @zhuhaozhe @blzheng @wenzhe-nrv @jiayisunx @ipiszy @kadeng @muchulee8 @amjames @chauhang @aak...

title: thrust sort/argsort silently produces wrong results when workspace allocation fails
body_excerpt: ## Summary `cupy.sort()` and `cupy.argsort()` can silently return incorrect results when GPU memory is under pressure and thrust workspace allocation fails. The root cause is that `cupy/cuda/thrust.pyx` declares `cupy_malloc()` as `noexcept with gil`. When `memory.alloc()` raises `OutOfMemoryError`, Cython swallows the exception, prints a warning to stderr, and returns NULL. The C++ allocator does not validate this NULL pointer, so thrust receives a garbage workspace buffer, silently corrupts the sort output, and returns normally without raising an exception. ## Expected Behavior `cupy.sort()` and `cupy.argsort()` should raise `OutOfMemoryError` when thrust workspace allocation fails, preventing silent data corruption. ## Actual Behavior When VRAM utilization crosses a threshold (varies by GPU architecture): - A message is printed to stderr: `Exception ignored in: 'cupy.cuda.thrust.cupy_malloc'` followed by the full `OutOfMemoryError` traceback - The `sort()` / `argsort()` call returns **without raising an exception** - The returned array contains **incorrect values** - Downstream computation silently uses corrupted results ## Environment | Property | Value | |----------|-------...

title: truncated_normal can't handle extreme bounds
body_excerpt: `jax.random.truncated_normal` produces deeply wrong results when you set the lower bound too high or the upper bound too low. Is it possible in JAX to somehow keep track of the number of replaced/clipped values? I've tried playing around with `value_and_grad` but couldn't figure out how to put information about the gradient into the function value. This may just be the same as #364, but I'm hoping that there's a workaround until that gets added. Context: I'm using JAX to estimate a model with maximum likelihood, so my objective is a sum of many log likelihoods. At some parameter values there can be overflow/underflow issues. One way to deal with this is to replace any invalid log likelihoods/derivatives with reasonable values to keep estimation going.

title: Inconsistent Reduction precision in backwards computation
body_excerpt: ### Description JAX implicitly upcasts BF16 inputs to `jnp.sum` to FP32 (see [here](https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/blob/955f96a453184441d6db11261eab40f24131b1ef/jax/_src/numpy/reductions.py#L231)). However, such reductions are also generated automatically in the backward pass for things like broadcasts. In this case, BF16 reductions are used, which can be highly unstable. This is inconsistent with the implicit upcasting of `jnp.sum`. In addition: reductions in matrix multiplication are also done in FP32. A simple example of the grad of a broadcast: ``` import jax import jax.numpy as jnp x = jnp.ones((128, 128), dtype=jnp.bfloat16) def f(x, a): out = jnp.sin(x * a).astype(jnp.float32) return jnp.sum(out) f_grad = jax.jit(jax.grad(f, argnums=(0, 1))) f_grad.lower(x, 2.3).as_text() ``` gives a BF16 reduction: ``` %8 = stablehlo.reduce(%7 init: %cst_0) applies stablehlo.add across dimensions = [0, 1] : (tensor<128x128xbf16>, tensor<bf16>) -> tensor<bf16> ``` FP32 upcasting for reductions should be used consistently (both for `jnp.sum` but also reductions in the backward pass), but ideally, should be controllable via a context manager. ### System info (python version, jaxlib version, ...

title: Add an `unroll` parameter to `while_loop`
body_excerpt: **Feature request:** Add an `unroll` parameter for [`while_loop`](https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/_autosummary/jax.lax.while_loop.html), like there is for [`scan`](https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/_autosummary/jax.lax.scan.html). Its purpose would be the same as for `scan`: To reduce the number of kernel launches, which slow things down on GPU. I personally use `while_loop` and experience this kind of slowdown. Below is an example implementation: ```python3 import jax import jax.numpy as jnp from jax import lax def unrolled_while_loop(cond_fun, body_fun, init_val, unroll=1): """ A statically unrolled version of jax.lax.while_loop. Executes `body_fun` speculatively `unroll` times per XLA while-loop iteration to reduce kernel launch overhead. It uses safe-state pre-masking to guarantee that terminal states do not produce NaNs during forward or backward passes. Args: cond_fun: Function `a -> bool` evaluating the loop condition. body_fun: Function `a -> a` computing the next state. init_val: Initial loop state (can be an arbitrary PyTree). unroll: Integer specifying how many times to unroll the body per iteration. Returns: The final terminal state of the loop. """ if unroll < 1: raise ...

title: isfinite(inf) raises FloatingPointError in vectorized functions
body_excerpt: The following works as expected: ```python @nb.njit def finite(x): return math.isfinite(x) ``` >>> finite(1.) True >>> finite(math.nan) False >>> finite(math.inf) False However, this vectorized version raises an exception when it receives inf: ```python @nb.vectorize def finite(x): return math.isfinite(x) ``` >>> finite(1.) True >>> finite(math.nan) False >>> finite(math.inf) FloatingPointError: invalid value encountered in finite It is interesting to notice that the behavior changes depending on np.seterr() settings: >>> np.seterr(all='raise') >>> finite(math.inf) FloatingPointError: invalid value encountered in finite [...] >>> np.seterr(all='warn') >>> finite(math.inf) RuntimeWarning: invalid value encountered in finite [...] False >>> np.seterr(all='ignore') >>> finite(math.inf) False The same happens in guvectorized functions. I understand isfinite(inf) should never raise an exception or warning, according to the behavior of math.isfinite() or np.isfinite(), or its own behavior in the non-vectorized version. Using Numba 0.60.0 and Python 3.10.12.

body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug Copied from #92043 which still applies for vectorized PPC and likely to ZArch while it was fixed for x86 by #93277 Pytorch wrongly returns nan for complex numbers division where the results are still within the range of the datatype. title: Support alpha=inf consistently for torch.celu
body_excerpt: The celu activation function introduced in https://arxiv.org/pdf/1704.07483 is described as being C1 differentiable across values of alpha. - for alpha -> inf it converges to the identity op (f(x) = x) - for alpha -> 0+ it converges to relu(x) = max(0, x) The Pytorch [celu](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/aten/src/ATen/native/Activation.cpp#L538-L549) (and related [quantized_celu](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/aten/src/ATen/native/quantized/cpu/qelu.cpp#L24)) ) implementation(s) appears to call a parameterized elu, following the celu definition, so it looks like it will have these properties within bounds of overflow. On the other hand I am not sure what the Pytorch behavior is intended to be in the implementation for alpha=0 and alpha=inf, but I think it would be nice to have it consistent. At alpha=0 it raises RuntimeError ZeroDivisionError, which is fine, though it seems could instead for alpha=0 just short-circuit to return relu(x). On the other hand, at alpha=torch.inf, positive values of x appear to return x, while non-positive values of x return `torch.nan`: ``` x = torch.tensor(2.) torch.celu(x, torch.inf) # tensor(2.) torch.celu(-x, torch.inf...

title: [MPS] Complex `abs` overflows/underflows with large/small inputs
github_labels: module: numerical-stability|triaged|module: complex|module: edge cases|module: mps|bot-triaged
body_excerpt: For sufficiently large or small complex inputs, the output of `torch.abs` for MPS overflows to inf or underflows to 0, whereas the CPU op does not. This is due to the fact that the formula that the MPS op uses is $\sqrt{\text{real}^2 + \text{imag}^2}$, so the square can overflow. Reproducer: ```python import torch a_cpu = torch.tensor( [ 1e-30 + 1e-30j, 1e32 + 1e32j, ], device='cpu', dtype=torch.cfloat, ) a_mps = a_cpu.to('mps') a_cpu_abs = a_cpu.abs() a_mps_abs = a_mps.abs() print(f'{a_cpu=}') print(f'{a_mps=}') print(f'{a_cpu_abs=}') print(f'{a_mps_abs=}') ``` Running the above gives: ``` a_cpu=tensor([1.0000e-30+1.0000e-30j, 1.0000e+32+1.0000e+32j]) a_mps=tensor([1.0000e-30+1.0000e-30j, 1.0000e+32+1.0000e+32j], device='mps:0') a_cpu_abs=tensor([1.4142e-30, 1.4142e+32]) a_mps_abs=tensor([0., inf], device='mps:0') ``` cc @ezyang @anjali411 @dylanbespalko @mruberry @nikitaved @amjames @kulinseth @malfet @DenisVieriu97 @jhavukainen @aditvenk

title: Ban GradScaler scale from being less than 1
body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch We should standardize on a way to tell users when a reasonable/good scale for the AMP GradScaler cannot be found. Context: The grad scaler is awesome in that it "automatically" finetunes itself to settle on an ideal scale. However! There are instances where there is just no ideal scale for certain parameters, for example the one mentioned in issue #96755, where the scale becomes so so tiny that it causes infs and, consequently, nans. In this issue, we were nestled in the unlikely (but clearly not impossible) world where for a certain scale S, the scaled gradients were valid, but the unscaled (g/S) were invalid, leading to weird inconsistent behavior. Generally, we want to be add invariants/guarantees to prevent weird inconsistent behavior and give users faster and clearer signal. Since the purpose of the scale is to scale UP the loss so that the grads do not underflow in fp16, we should set a hard boundary of scale must be greater than or equal to 1. Note that adding a check may induce a slight perf hit. cc @mcarilli @ptrblck @leslie-fang-intel @jgong5 @ngimel @crcrpar @stas00 @albanD ### Alternatives Do nothing, let users deal with nans f...

title: Deprecate and remove `convert_dtype` kwarg
body_excerpt: Many functions and methods in `cuml` currently take an underdocumented `convert_dtype` kwarg. For example, `LogisticRegression.fit`: ``` convert_dtype : bool, optional (default = True) When set to True, the train method will, when necessary, convert y to be the same data type as X if they differ. This will increase memory used for the method. ``` The true behavior is method/function specific, but in most cases actually has the following behavior: - Most methods support 1 or more valid dtypes, (e.g. `float32` and `float64`). Most methods also require all arrays have the same input dtype (we only have a few that support mixed precision). - If `convert_dtype=True` (the default), all inputs will be converted to one of the valid dtypes as needed (with a copy). Additionally all inputs will be normalized to be of the same dtype (as needed), usually following the dtype of `X`. - If `convert_dtype=False`, things just error if the input dtypes aren't exact. title: jnp.log/log2/log10 return -inf for subnormal float32 inputs (XLA DAZ flush)
body_excerpt: ### Description `jnp.log`, `jnp.log2`, and `jnp.log10` return `-inf` for subnormal `float32` inputs on the CPU backend, while NumPy returns the correct finite negative values. body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch Currently `softmax` handles `-inf` in most of the cases, for example: ```python >>> x = torch.tensor([-float('inf'), 1]) >>> x.softmax(-1) tensor([0., 1.]) >>> x.cuda().softmax(-1) tensor([0., 1.], device='cuda:0') ``` However, once the normalized dimension is comprised of solely `-inf`, there is an issue: ```python >>> x = torch.tensor([-float('inf')] * 2) >>> x.softmax(-1) tensor([nan, nan]) >>> x.cuda().softmax(-1) tensor([nan, nan], device='cuda:0') ``` I understand we get it because `inf - inf = nan`, but why not assume that `softmax` is computed in the limit? In such a case `softmax` should return a uniform distribution. This case is quite easy to detect since `max == -inf` will imply a uniform distribution. Issues for more context: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/25110 https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/103749 https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/103963 cc @albanD @mruberry @jbschlosser @walterddr @mikaylagawarecki

title: Ctx or at least Thread level switch for fp32 IEEE precision tolerance
body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch Right now fp precision switching is only possible at the `process` level via the following api: ```python torch.backends.fp32_precision = mode torch.backends.cuda.matmul.fp32_precision = mode torch.backends.cudnn.fp32_precision = mode torch.backends.cudnn.conv.fp32_precision = mode torch.backends.cudnn.rnn.fp32_precision = mode ``` With Python 3.13/3.14 and `GIL=0` threads, it is now possile to do everything `torch.distributed` can do but using threads instead of processes. Without a `ctx` or `thread` level toggle for `fp` precision, it not possible to have different threads doing different tasks. For example, an `inference` thread does not need high precision whereas a `quantization` thread which often need fp32 or higher accumulation will need full `ieee` precision. They cannot co-exist currently in torch due to this limitation. ### Alternatives Use `processes`. However, this is not a true alternative since with Python 3.14, we have stable `nogil` threads that can do concurrent work as efficiently if not more so than `processes`. cc @svekars @sekyondaMeta @AlannaBurke @ptrblck @msaroufim @eqy @jerryzh168 @albanD @pragupta

body_excerpt: Claude-generated description of the issue and repro: ``` """Minimal repro: cudf-polars streaming-mode broadcast bug for `with_columns(pl.lit(<numpy_array>))` at >~1M rows. body_excerpt: ## Problem SHAP tests currently use hard-coded expected values for assertions, making them brittle and prone to false failures when: - Algorithm implementations are updated or optimized - Random seed behavior changes across library versions - Numerical precision differs slightly across platforms or CUDA versions - Natural variance in Monte Carlo methods (like kernel SHAP) occurs ## Impact - Tests fail on legitimate code changes that don't affect correctness - Requires manual investigation to determine if failures are meaningful - Slows down development velocity - Creates uncertainty about whether changes introduce real bugs ## Proposed Solution Replace hard-coded assertions with statistical or tolerance-based checks: 1. **Use tolerance-based comparisons** instead of exact values: ```python # Instead of: assert shap_values[0] == 0.123 assert abs(shap_values[0] - expected) < tolerance ``` 2. **Compare against reference implementation**: ```python assert np.allclose(cuml_shap, sklearn_shap, rtol=0.05) ``` 3. **Test properties rather than values**: - SHAP values sum to prediction difference - Feature importance ordering is consistent - Values are within reasonable bounds 4. **Use st...

title: [Bug] ONNX Softmax/LogSoftmax/Hardmax frontend ignores opset <13 semantics
body_excerpt: ## Description The ONNX frontend converter for `Softmax`, `LogSoftmax`, and `Hardmax` only implements `_impl_v13`. It does not implement `_impl_v1` or `_impl_v11`, which have **different semantics** from v13. This causes **silently wrong results** when importing any ONNX model with opset version ≤12. ### ONNX spec difference - **Opset < 13**: The input is coerced to 2D by flattening at `axis` (default 1). Softmax is computed on the last dimension. The result is reshaped back to the original shape. - **Opset ≥ 13**: Softmax is computed directly along `axis` (default -1). No flattening. For a 3D input (2,3,4) with default axis, opset 11 computes softmax over the flattened last 2 dims (12 elements), while opset 13 computes softmax over the last dim (4 elements). These produce very different results. ## Reproduction ```python import numpy as np import onnx from onnx import helper, TensorProto import onnxruntime as ort shape = (2, 3, 4) X = np.random.randn(*shape).astype(np.float32) X_info = helper.make_tensor_value_info("X", TensorProto.FLOAT, list(shape)) Y_info = helper.make_tensor_value_info("Y", TensorProto.FLOAT, list(shape)) node = helper.make_node("Softmax", ["X"], ["Y"]) gra...

title: document why jnp.arange (like np.arange) is unsafe with `step`
body_excerpt: The NumPy docs explain why using `np.arange` with the `step` argument is difficult to use correctly. As @jewillco observed, it's even more dangerous with the lower-precision dtypes that JAX users might employ (like fp8 and bf16). So we should: 1. add a note to the `jnp.arange` docs warning about the dangers (perhaps mainly pointing to the NumPy docs' explanation), and 2. suggest an additional workaround not involving linspace (i.e. just write an expression like `(jnp.arange(-600, 600, dtype=float) * .01).astype(jnp.bfloat16)`.

title: Disentangle "jax_enable_x64" and default dtype
body_excerpt: ### Description Providing a way to enable `float64` without changing the default dtype/precision. Or even better, adding the option to choose the default dtype. For example, ```python jax.config.update('jax_enable_x64', True) jax.config.update('jax_default_dtype', jnp.float32) ``` ### Motivation Some algorithms, such as fast Fourier transforms and conjugate gradient methods, are unstable at 32-bit precision. It is therefore recommended to apply them at 64-bit precision. If such algorithms are part of some bigger procedure, the entire procedure must run at 64-bit precision. This is very wasteful, especially if the procedure involves neural networks. The current solution is to rewrite the procedure while explicitly requesting the `float32` dtype at **every** array creation. For large code bases, this is very tedious and it prevents the use of most libraries. ### Alternatives An even better solution would be to be able to set the dtype locally (e.g. with contexts), but I suspect that this would not play well with tracers.

body_excerpt: In *Evaluating Derivatives* (Griewank & Walther, §13) the Taylor series in the Taylor propagation approach (i.e., `jet`) is $f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n x^n,$ where $a_n$ is called the *n*-th Taylor coefficient. `jax.experimental.jet` instead propagates the factorial-scaled value $c_n=n! \cdot a_n$ and calls $c_n$ as the Taylor coefficient in the docs. While this makes the output of `jet` interpretable as an ordinary n-th order derivative of $f$, it forces extra scaling/un-scaling by \$n!\$, which can overflow or amplify rounding error due to the use of factorial (see #9712); **Proposal:** propagate the unscaled coefficients \$a\_n\$ internally and (optionally) offer a compatibility flag/wrapper current for the `n!` convention. Below is a comparison of the exponential rule before and after this change: ```python # Current jet implementation def _exp_taylor(primals_in, series_in, **_): x, = primals_in series, = series_in u = [x] + series v = [lax.exp(x)] + [None] * len(series) for k in range(1,len(v)): v[k] = fact(k-1) * sum(_scale(k, j) * v[k-j] * u[j] for j in range(1, k+1)) primal_out, *series_out = v return primal_out, series_out jet_rules[lax.exp_p] = _exp_taylor ``` ```pyt...

title: `jnp.sinc`'s gradient has large errors
body_excerpt: ### Description The current `jnp.sinc` which uses ```python return _where(eq_zero, _sinc_maclaurin(0, pi_x), lax.div(lax.sin(safe_pi_x), safe_pi_x)) ``` has large errors on its gradients when `x` and thus `safe_pi_x` is close to zero. To see why, note that $$ \frac{d}{dx}\frac{\sin(x)}{x} = \frac{1}{x}\left( \cos(x) - \frac{sin(x)}{x} \right) $$ When $x \approx 0$, Both $\cos(x)$ and $\frac{sin(x)}{x}$ are slightly smaller than 1 and have error of magnitude $u$ = `jnp.finfo(x.dtype).epsneg`. So the error of $\frac{d}{dx}\frac{\sin(x)}{x} \approx -\frac{x}{3}$ has absolute error of magnitude $\frac{u}{x}$ and relative error of magnitude $\frac{3u}{x ^ 2}$ which can be very large when $x \approx 0$. We can solve the issue by using `_sinc_maclaurin` for values near 0 instead of just 0 and using higher order taylor series for `_sinc_maclaurin`. The truncated Maclaurin series of $$ \frac{d}{dx}\frac{\sin(x)}{x} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{(-1)^i}{(2i+1)(2i-1)!} x^{2i-1} $$ has error term of magnitude $\frac{x^{2n+1}}{(2n+3)(2n+1)!}$ when $\lvert x \rvert$ is small. title: Should gradients of logsumexp([-inf, -inf]) be 0s instead NaNs?
body_excerpt: Consider this snippet ```python import jax import jax.numpy as jnp def f(x): return jax.nn.logsumexp(jnp.stack([-jnp.inf, -jnp.inf + x])) jax.grad(f)(1.) ``` The computation inside `f` is essentially what happens inside the dynamic program of the CTC loss and similar losses that calculates a shortest distance over the log semiring. There, `-jnp.inf` is really "log(0)", and we can see that `(0 + 0 * exp(x))`'s gradient w.r.t. `x` should indeed be 0. Right now, the gradients are NaN instead because the gradients of `logsumexp([-inf, -inf])` are NaNs.

title: Speed regression in 0.29.0
body_excerpt: Referring to the discussion in #2176 it looks like there is a major speed regression from 0.28.1 to 0.29.0. The example function below and similar tight loops, doing merely more than nan checks, additions etc, only run at a fraction of the initial speed. title: Refactor precision handling in test/test_optim.py
body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch Currently, there are scattered places in the optimizer tests that reduce precision (grepping for `atol` or `rtol` in the file will take you to those places). Since optimizers are a composition of ATen ops, they reasonably require higher tolerances. Thus, we should establish a per optimizer (and perhaps per dtype) tolerance at the top level of the test file and use that everywhere. This consolidation has (at least) two functions: - Define an agreed upon set of expected tolerances for optimizers - Enable ease when writing new optimizer tests that will inevitably run into the same tolerance issues. One way to do this is to override assertEqual in the Optimizer TestCase class. ### Alternatives Another way is to globally define them and then pass them whenever needed. This seems a more manual way to get the same results as overriding though. ### Additional context I'm in the middle of migrating tests from test/optim/test_optim.py to test/test_optim.py. title: MX basic dtypes in pytorch/pytorch
body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch # Overview The Open Compute Project introduced the [MicroScaling formats (MX)](https://www.opencompute.org/documents/ocp-microscaling-formats-mx-v1-0-spec-final-pdf) in Sep 2023, defining block-scaled dtypes with E8M0 block scales and FP8|FP6|FP4|INT8 block elements. We propose adding the E8M0 and FP4 dtypes from the MX spec to pytorch/pytorch. We expect the derived dtype logic (combining scales + data) and the modeling logic for converting a high precision model to use MX to live outside of pytorch/pytorch. body_excerpt: DeepSeek mentions that they keep optimizer states in bf16, this is something that afaik our optimizers don't support. title: [MPS] For accumulating ops allow the correctness tolerance to scale within the envelope of the reference implementations drift
body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug ### Context Related to the discussion at issue #182817 this is an orthogonal issue with the current testing approach and a suggestion on how we could address it: When testing op correctness for fp16/bf16 implementations in MPS backend we compare against the CPU computations done with the same precision. For ops that aggregate multiple computations to produce the elements of the final result like convolutions or reduction ops the ordering how the computation happens will cause a drift in the final product. One can estimate the worst case per-element error with `err = sqrt(K) * eps * |x|` where `K` is the reduction depth, `eps` the machine epsilon for the dtype and `|x|` the partial product magnitude. title: Raise exception when torch.clamp min value underflows the input tensor's dtype
body_excerpt: Consider the following code: ```python x = torch.relu(torch.randn(10)) x = torch.clamp(x, min=1e-8) y = 100 / x ``` The code above runs just fine when `x.dtype == torch.float` but fails when `x.dtype == torch.half`. The error is that 1e-8 can't be represented in fp16 and silently underflows to 0. Depending on the network it can be difficult to track down the source of this class of error (especially if a network was originally written assuming fp32 and is then trained with mixed precision). Could we validate inputs for potential underflows and raise an exception if one is detected?

title: feat(examples): implement vllm in triton
body_excerpt: Vllm uses paged memory and has kernels that perform the generation part of the causal inference. The computation pattern of generation part - single Q for entire seq len of KV - is very different from computing the context part (which benefits from seq length parallelism over Q and hence flash attention). In this case, the bottleneck should be memory, as the KV values cannot be reused over the Q seq len, so it is an interesting question to ask how to tradeoff latency and parallelism with compute efficiency. In this case, batching similar seq length inference is very important. I also wonder if distributed shared memory and TMA optimizations would be beneficial here since it is so memory-bottlenecked. It would be interesting to implement this in triton and see whether triton can match or exceed the performance. Reference VLLM implementation here: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/d2b2eed67c49cdda3c1d6fa09ee2ec128b318138/csrc/attention/attention_kernels.cu#L32

body_excerpt: ## Motivation The following work is done jointly by me and my team @kaitingwang at Huawei Canada. The TritonGPUCoalesce pass generates blocked layouts for load/stores that favour memory coalescing and vectorization. However, we have observed in certain cases the blocked layout generate by TritonGPUCoalesce pass is suboptimal and results in generation of `convert_layout` instructions. When these `convert_layout` are generated inside a loop, it could negatively impact performance. title: TritonAMDGPUPipeline crash with 4+ loads and num_stages=4
body_excerpt: ### Describe the bug Note: I had Claude Code narrow down the issue and create this reproducer. Apologies for any AI hallucinations. The Triton AMD GPU software pipeliner crashes during compilation when num_stages=4 and the kernel loop body contains 4+ loads combined with dot products and online softmax (exp/maximum operations). The crash occurs in the `tritonamdgpu-schedule-loops{num_stages=4}` pass of the `TritonAMDGPUPipeline`. The MLIR error is: ``` 'tt.load' op operation destroyed but still has uses LLVM ERROR: operation destroyed but still has uses ``` This is an MLIR use-after-erase bug: the pipeliner erases a `tt.load` op during loop schedule restructuring, but that op's SSA value is still referenced by a downstream consumer (typically an `arith.extf` or similar type conversion feeding into a `tl.dot` or addition). ### Characteristics - Specific to num_stages=4. Stages 1-3 and 5-8 all compile fine. - Requires 4+ loads in the loop body. 3 loads is fine. - Requires the loads to feed into dot products + softmax-like arithmetic (exp, maximum, accumulation). 4 loads with simple accumulation is fine. - Independent of block sizes (tested 16x16 through 64x64). - Independent of dt...

title: dot_product_attention has inconsistent dot types in backward pass
body_excerpt: ### Description `jax.nn.dot_product_attention` does the first dot product with `preferred_element_type=jnp.float32` (see [here](https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/blob/7f655972c47658768b6ecce752fa29c3a64a824a/jax/_src/nn/functions.py#L846)). title: Implicit dtype promotion for float8 and int4
body_excerpt: We've had several requests to add implicit promotion semantics for float8, int4, and friends. What do i mean by this? Currently, if you try to combine `float8` with other float dtypes in binary operations, you get an error: ```python >>> jnp.float8_e3m4(1) + jnp.bfloat16(1) TypePromotionError: Input dtypes ('bfloat16', 'float8_e3m4') have no available implicit dtype promotion path. To avoid unintended promotion, 8-bit floats do not support implicit promotion. If you'd like your inputs to be promoted to another type, you can do so explicitly using e.g. x.astype('float32') ``` This was a deliberate design choice: when we first added narrow-width floats and ints, our assumption was that they would mostly be used in very particular settings, e.g. as inputs to device-specific matmul kernels, and users would benefit from having guard-rails against inadvertent type promotion. But increasingly this hard line is causing issues for users: for example, pallas has had to implement this helper to work around the lack of implicit promotion for int4 and float8: https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/blob/3ebff21919983f87ce5dcab4cc0b27eb89b28368/jax/_src/pallas/primitives.py#L705-L711 This issue tracks ...

title: [CUDA][CUDACachingAllocator] size overflow in caching_allocator_alloc raises SystemError for size >= 2**63
github_labels: module: cuda|module: error checking|triaged|module: edge cases
body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug ### Describe the bug `torch.cuda.memory.caching_allocator_alloc()` raises a `SystemError` when the requested allocation size is `2**63`. For `2**63 - 1`, it raises a normal CUDA out-of-memory `RuntimeError`. For `2**63`, it raises: ```text SystemError: _cuda_cudaCachingAllocator_raw_alloc returned a result with an exception set ``` I think this is not expected behavior. Even if the requested allocation size is invalid or too large, this API should raise a clean Python exception such as `OverflowError`, `ValueError`, or a normal CUDA OOM `RuntimeError`, not `SystemError`. This may be related to #177827, but it does not seem to be the same issue. #177827 is about negative allocation sizes, while this issue is triggered by a positive size larger than `PY_SSIZE_T_MAX`. ### Minimal reproduction ```python import torch import traceback print("torch:", torch.__version__) print("cuda available:", torch.cuda.is_available()) print("device:", torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)) for size in [2**63 - 1, 2**63]: print("\nsize =", size) try: ptr = torch.cuda.memory.caching_allocator_alloc(size, device=0) print("allocated:", ptr) torch.cuda.memory.caching_allocator_delete(ptr) ...

title: [MPS] Switch test_output_match / test_output_grad_match to magnitude-floored relative tolerance
body_excerpt: ## Context `test/test_mps.py::TestConsistencyMPS::test_output_match` and `test_output_grad_match` compare MPS vs CPU output element-wise via `assertEqual(cpu_out, mps_out, atol=atol, rtol=rtol)`. The tolerance pair comes from `_compute_tolerances(op, dtype)` plus a chain of inline overrides. The standard `assertEqual` check is `|a - b| <= atol + rtol * |b|`. When a tensor has a single near-zero output element (very common for special functions near a pole, gradients of `grid_sampler_2d` at boundary cells, reductions over inputs that nearly cancel, etc.), `rtol * |b|` collapses to ~0 and a 1-ULP absolute diff trips the assertion even though the rest of the tensor is fine. title: Int32 overflow in bincount indexing
body_excerpt: ## 🐛 Bug In `aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/SummaryOps.cu`, there is a snippet: ``` template<typename input_t, typename IndexType> __device__ static IndexType getBin(input_t bVal, input_t minvalue, input_t maxvalue, int nbins) { IndexType bin = (int)((bVal - minvalue) * nbins / (maxvalue - minvalue)); ``` When data type is int32, for big enough value of bVal and big number of nbins, multiplication causes int overflow that can result in negative bin index returned. This can cause memory corruption. ## To Reproduce Steps to reproduce the behavior: 1. Run bincount with minval=0, nbins=65536, and value 36830 inside. title: [BUG] [DEBT] THROW macro is unsafe
body_excerpt: **Describe the bug** The [`THROW`](https://github.com/rapidsai/cuml/blob/branch-0.10/cpp/src_prims/utils.h#L84) macro is using a fixed size buffer to form the message for an exception. title: [TASK] Review types used for size and indexing throughout codebase
body_excerpt: As noted in discussion on #4075, there are currently places in the codebase where we are using signed integers for positive indexing or to represent container sizes or other quantities that are better represented by other types (generally `std::size_t`). In order to clearly signal the semantic meaning of these variables, avoid signed/unsigned casting and comparisons, and to reduce the likelihood of overflow/underflow bugs, I propose the following rules: 1. Avoid raw indexed loops wherever possible, instead giving preference to the relevant STL algorithm 2. Always represent the size of an STL container with `some_container<T>::size_type` and use the same type for raw positive indexing. Liberal use of `auto` should make this less onerous, and rule 1 should make it rare. 3. When representing the size of a quantity *other* than the size of a container or doing any other kind of raw positive indexing, use `std::size_t` *unless* there is a clear performance/resource reason to use a smaller type. body_excerpt: Many of cuml's tests are aimed at comparing results between different implementations, e.g., the GPU and CPU implementation of the same estimator and against third-party implementations, notably scikit-learn. We expect estimators to overall behave very similarly and their results to be identical up to numerical precision. Further, estimators are usually tested only against a specific combination of inputs and example datasets, an approach that likely fails to test rare edge cases and cannot provide confidence for the equivalence of a wide-range of inputs and datasets. title: RTNE semantics are not respected by `tt.fp_to_fp` going from f16 to f8e5m2 on A100
body_excerpt: ### Describe the bug Using `tt.fp_to_fp` with `rtne` semantics on A100 to convert `f16` to `f8e5m2` yields wrong results. For instance, `9` rounds to `10` instead of the expected `8` Doing the job of rounding manually using additional guard-round-sticky bits for convenience, we have the following representations for 8, 9 and 10 in `f8e5m2`: ``` 01001000|000 // 8 01001000|100 // 9 01001001|000 // 10 ``` According to round-to-nearest-even semantics, when only the guard bit is set, we should round to make the last bit of the mantissa even. In this case, this means rounding down. The bit-twiddling algorithm used for conversion on A100 therefore seems wrong. ### Environment details GPU: A100

title: Numerical Discrepancies between Pallas Kernel and Standard JAX with bfloat16
body_excerpt: ### Description We are observing small numerical differences between a JAX function compiled with @jax.jit and an equivalent operation implemented as a Pallas kernel when using jnp.bfloat16 data types. The operations involve taking the mean of the squares of a tiled 2D array row-wise, followed by a reciprocal square root. While all intermediate computations within both versions are explicitly cast to jnp.float32, the final results, when cast back to jnp.bfloat16, show differences in a small number of elements. The standard JAX version and the Pallas kernel version produce bit-identical results when the input and output types are jnp.float32. The discrepancies only appear when downcasting the float32 results to jnp.bfloat16. We suspect this might be due to slightly different floating-point summation orders within the jnp.mean operation between XLA's standard optimization and the Pallas/Mosaic tiled execution, leading to minute differences in the float32 results. These differences, although small in float32, cross rounding boundaries when converting to bfloat16, especially after being transformed by lax.rsqrt. title: [FEA] Optimize str.split().list.get() via fused lazy extraction (~160x speedup observed)

title: [TASK] Increase parallelism or sparse normalization prims
body_excerpt: Cuml has CSR-based primitives that contain kernels, both in Python and in C, which currently map each row of the CSR to a single thread and loop over the columns serially to perform L1/l2/l_inf normalization. The performance and the parallelism, including the sums, could be made much more parallel if we map the individual rows to warps with a block size set to something like the average degree. The current method might be the best option when the average degree is extremely small but as the average degree grows larger, the parallelism can be increased significantly, while also enabling coalesced reads (and potentially even writes in the case of normalization where all the values need to be modified).

title: tl.trans on fp8 (byte) types produces 6.5x performance regression on AMDGPU since triton 3.4.0
body_excerpt: # tl.trans on fp8 (byte) types produces 6.5x performance regression on AMDGPU since triton 3.4.0 ## Summary `tl.trans` on `float8e4nv` tiles followed by a store to column-major output produces severely non-coalesced memory writes on AMDGPU (gfx942 / MI300X) starting from triton 3.4.0. The same code runs 6.5x faster on triton 3.3.1. ## Root Cause The frontend fails to mark a stride of 1 as a constexpr when annotated with `: int`. title: [RFC] Adding posit/bfloat16/float9 to VTA data path
body_excerpt: Feature proposal: add posit/bfloat16/float9 as data types to the VTA data path We would like to add different floating point types to the VTA data path so that VTA can be used to study learning rates and recall accuracy across a variety of number systems. Posits are a tapered floating point system providing independent control over precision and dynamic range. Bfloat16 is the Brain Floating Point Format that Google introduced in its TPUs float9 is the format that Microsoft introduced in its project BrainWave We are seeking feedback from the community on the design and integration of new number systems into the VTA instruction set and micro-architecture.

title: [CodeGen] LLVM codegen doesn't respect mfloat-abi=hard
body_excerpt: For versions of LLVM < 6.0, the mfloat-abi=hard flag does not appear to be respected resulting in operators such as exp and softmax giving incorrect results on Raspberry Pi 3. This issue is discussed [here](https://discuss.tvm.ai/t/softmax-layer-not-working-on-raspberry-pi-4/4191). I've tested with LLVM versions 4.0, 5.0 and 6.0 and only 6.0 gives the correct result. I've got a small patch (PR: [4071](https://github.com/dmlc/tvm/pull/4071)) to throw a fatal error in the case of trying to use mfloat-abi=hard with a version of LLVM < 6.0 so that this problem isn't silent.

title: Gradient of SVD with degenerate singular values becomes NaN
body_excerpt: If an SVD has degenerate singular values (multiple entries of S are exactly equal), the gradient pass will give `nan`. This is because the [AD formula](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.02659.pdf) contains something like `1 / (s[i] ** 2 - s[j] ** 2) ` which becomes `nan` if `s[i] == s[j]`. There are also terms with `1 / S` which become 'nan' if any of 'S' is zero. In particular, this situation arises when multiple singular values are `0.0`. and it evaluates the entire gradient of a function to `nan`, even if the function does not depend on the rows of U and columns of V that correspond to the `0.0` singular values (See example below). Essentially in this case, even if the adjoint gradients of the corresponding slices of U and V are `0.`, they are multiplied by `nan` and thus give `nan`. I don't have a clear vision, what the best case scenario is here. I just wanted to share that this problem arises for me and how i will dirty-fix it. body_excerpt: It seems like check_grads has incorrect scaling behaviour for large input tensors. body_excerpt: ### Description The current L-BFGS implementation (`jax._src.scipy.optimize._lbfgs`) has several robustness issues compared to scipy's `L-BFGS-B` that cause it to fail on non-trivial optimization problems. Missing `old_old_fval` in line search** The BFGS implementation already tracks `old_old_fval` and passes it to the line search for adaptive initial step size estimation (see `bfgs.py` line 121, 138, 169). body_excerpt: **Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.** There are numerous places in cudf that require polymorphic behavior depending on the dtype of a parameter. Two of the most prominent are `ColumnBase.astype` and `build_column`, both of which essentially boil down to a switch statement based on the dtype. There are numerous issues with this implementation. title: [BUG] Treelite format needs to be updated to accommodate 32-bit and 64-bit floats
body_excerpt: **Describe the bug** #837 added Treelite as a submodule. Currently, Treelite uses single-precision floating-point (`float`) to store test thresholds and leaf outputs in decision trees. This is good for XGBoost models, but however, some other packages such as LightGBM use double-precision floating-point (`double`). **Steps/Code to reproduce bug** See dmlc/treelite#98, dmlc/treelite#95, where Treelite is not able to match prediction results for LightGBM models. Due to semantics of floating-point numbers, there is always truncation whenever we convert between `float` and `double`. As part of 1.0 release of Treelite (dmlc/treelite#111), I'd like to propose an update to the exchange format to support multiple data types. This way, the Treelite exchange format will represent LightGBM models faithfully. I'll post an update when a concrete proposal is ready. @canonizer

title: [FEA] Check convergence before setting fit_status for SVM
body_excerpt: **Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.** In Sklearn, the fit_status variable of SVM's indicate the following: - 0 means correctly fitted - 1 otherwise, which can also mean that the model is fitted but it did not converge up to the required precision. - The variable is not defined before we fit the model In cuML, currently we have the following implementation: - 0 means fitted, more precisely the fit method returned succesfully. It can still happen that the training was terminated because of reaching `max_iter`, which means that we did not reach the required tolerance. - The variable is not defined before we fit the model **Describe the solution you'd like** Set the fit status to be consistent with Sklearn. We have the number of iterations and the reached tolerance (`diff`) after the solver finished. https://github.com/rapidsai/cuml/blob/396fc69e58800310e2b0de8e3017cf85e4d77207/cpp/src/svm/smosolver.h#L161-L164 We could for example return `n_iter` from SmoSolver in the SvmModel struct, and compare it to max_iter in the python layer to check whether the exit criteria was reaching max iter.

title: [BUG] `matrixVectorOp` in `Dbscan::Vertexdeg::Algo` should set `bcastAlongRows` as false
body_excerpt: **Describe the bug** A clear and concise description of what the bug is. IIUC, in `Dbscan::Vertexdeg::Algo` we hope to apply normalization to the input matrix when using cosine metric. However, in the current implementation (v23.06), with `bcastAlongRows = true` passed to `raft::linalg::matrixVectorOp`, it actually does something not as we expect, like: ``` for i in [0..nLines) and j in [0..lineLen): out[i, j] = op(in[i, j], row_norm[j]) where matrix indexing is row-major ([i, j] = [i * lineLen + j]) ``` Obviously, the columns are mistakenly divided by the l2 norm of each row with same index. We should do it by crossing rows instead of along rows. Moreover, if the size of rows is smaller than the size of columns, UB occurs because of access to an illegal memory. title: [FEA] Changing `COO` `Index_Type` in UMAP to prevent overflow when running with large datasets
body_excerpt: ### Description UMAP cannot run large datasets right now because of an overflow issue. `raft::sparse::COO` defaults to using `int` for its `Index_Type` and this becomes a problem. When [this issue](https://github.com/rapidsai/raft/issues/2405) is solved, we need to update `UMAPAlgo::FuzzySimplSet::ML::run()` to take `COO` with an `Index_Type` other than `int`. ### Details Specifically, `coo_symmetrize` (raft function called from `UMAPAlgo::FuzzySimplSet::ML::run()`) allocates `nnz * 2` space on device. For a large dataset (e.g. 88M samples with knn graph degree 16) this value is larger than max int (88M * 16 * 2 > INT_MAX).

title: [TRACKER] Cleanup python estimator implementations
body_excerpt: I've been (slowly) working through our list of estimators applying a set of common cleanups. Rather than open an issue for each estimator I figured I'd open a tracker issue instead. I view this work as half paying down tech-debt and half fixing bugs. Each estimator has their own warts, but in general we're interested in applying the following actions to each estimator: - Simplifying `__init__`. Estimators should have a simple `__init__`. No hyperparameters should be validated or mutated in `__init__`, any validation/modification needed should happen at the time of use in e.g. `fit`. See [the sklearn docs](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/developers/develop.html#instantiation) for more here. An `__init__` should just set attributes for all hyperparameters and return, nothing more. This also includes removing setting fitted attributes to `None` in `__init__`. There's no reason to do this. - Removing mutation of hyperparameters elsewhere in the model. If a value should be inferred/thresholded/amended in some way, that should happen locally in e.g. `fit` and leave the original value unmodified. title: UMAP spectral initialization outputs nans
body_excerpt: For the example below UMAP output embedding produces nan values. ## Findings so far `init='random'` works but `init='spectral'` does not. Confirmed that the issue is coming from spectral embedding. Commenting out everything beyond spectral embedding still shows nans. https://github.com/rapidsai/cuml/blob/main/cpp/src/umap/runner.cuh#L331C1-L345C40 Found the root cause which is a divide by zero problem during laplacian normalization step. title: [BUG] HoltWinters - issues in HoltWinters Optimization
body_excerpt: There are several issues in HoltWinters Optimization when optimizing alpha, beta, and gamma values: 1. Precision - There's an instability when using floating points. For example, floating points work fine when the training dataset has big numbers (say, 300 and upwards) and obtain the same answers as double points. However, if you normalize these values to be between 0 and 1, floating point optimization fails and does not give the same accuracy as a test run with double point on the same dataset. There are gtests documenting this on the cpp side, in `cuml/cpp/src/test/sg/holtwinters_test.cu` for reference. 2. Epsilon - While not exactly a bug, the value of epsilon still vastly determines how well optimization occurs. Taking the above example of our non-normalized dataset, we do not get the same accuracy unless floating point epsilon is in the range `1e-3` and double epsilon is in the range `1e-7`. 3. Line Search Iter Limit - If line search iter limit is reached while doing a BFGS optimization, wrong values for next params are being updated. Basically, the ones which minimize loss should be chosen but they are not. These issues will be mentioned in the relevant areas of the code.

title: [Bug] Padded, quantized convolution operators give incorrect results on edges
body_excerpt: When the microTVM team was working on our submission for MLPerf Tiny, we noticed the `kws` model had slightly worse accuracy than expected (we classified `897/1000` samples correctly, while folks are expected to classify [at least `900/1000` correctly](https://github.com/mlcommons/tiny/tree/master/benchmark)). The bug has been remarkably hard to track down. We have a bunch of [end-to-end operator](https://github.com/apache/tvm/tree/main/tests/python/relay/strategy/arm_cpu/) tests, and our results match exactly with those in other parts of TVM. I originally thought this was a padding issue, but that didn't pan out. It turns out the issue is caused by a bugged optimization for re-quantization. This issue only occurs in quantization (which is why our tests didn't catch it - those don't include quantization steps), and only on the edges of padded tensors (which explains why it hurt accuracy slightly, but not a ton). I've written up an explanation of the issue below. cc @alanmacd @areusch @gromero @mehrdadh @mkatanbaf

title: [RFC] ProcessGroupNCCL uses non-blocking API by default
body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch ## Motivation: - Gives better fault tolerance against hangs in comm init, comm destroy and P2P operations (involves dynamic connection performed by CPU). - Allow overlap between NCCL init and other stuff users want the main thread to do (e.g., model or data loader init) Here "non-blocking" refers to whether a NCCL API call would immediately return or block the host CPU (Traditionally, some NCCL APIs such as ncclCommInitRank may block for a little when rendezvous is performed.) title: dict_tag optimization leads to wrong results with relational guards
body_excerpt: ### 🐛 Describe the bug `dict_tag` optimization checks if a dictionary that we guard on has changed or not and if all the values in it are immutable, no further processing is done on the dictionary if the tag is the same. This avoids running a lot of guards on the dictionary and its values and makes the C++ guards faster. However this assumes that running a guard has no side-effects. This is true for almost all cases except for RelationalGuards which do keep a state. In RelationalGuards, we need 2 values for the guards and the way it works is that the guard returns True for the first run, stores the first value in the guard and only returns True or False in the last run. When a guard is not run because of dict_tag optimization, this leads to false positives. Eg: ```python import torch a = torch.randn(5).cuda() d = {"a": a} def fn(a, d): return a is d["a"], torch.sum(a) cfn = torch.compile(fn) print(cfn(a, d)[0]) print(cfn(a.clone(), d)[0]) ``` Above prints `True` in both cases because of the dict_tag optimization. (`a is d["a"]` is a object aliasing guard which is a relational guard.) In https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/139899, I disabled the dict_tag optimization when Rel...

title: Place data on CPU memory for `nn_descent` option in HDBSCAN
body_excerpt: Current implementation of HDBSCAN puts data on GPU memory at the python layer. https://github.com/rapidsai/cuml/blob/e05c9a5b1750ff1c145746441eff563ee0fa90ed/python/cuml/cuml/cluster/hdbscan/hdbscan.pyx#L916-L928 NN-Descent always copies the input data to GPU memory, even if the user originally provides it on the GPU. This is required because the algorithm internally converts the data to FP16. As a result, providing GPU-resident data leads to duplicate GPU allocations and unnecessary memory usage. Therefore, when using the `nn_descent option, the input data should be put on CPU memory to avoid this extra GPU-side copy.

title: [FEA] In-place k-select for sparse knn on string matching
body_excerpt: One of the challenges with providing optimized primitives for sparse datasets is the large number of different degree distributions that can be encountered in practice. In some recent discussions with @teju85 @beckernick @VibhuJawa @aerdem4 and @randerzander, we have isolated some potential upper bounds specific to the string matching use-case which can offer some additional memory savings (and potential performance boost) by performing the k-select in the same kernel that's computing distances. title: [RFC][Datatypes] Bring Your Own Datatypes: supporting custom (software) datatypes
body_excerpt: See the custom datatypes pull request at #2900. This RFC proposes support for custom datatypes. Specifically, we only propose supporting software datatypes at the moment. By "software datatype", we mean a datatype (e.g. a [posit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unum_(number_format)#Type_III_Unum_-_Posit)) which is implemented by a library (e.g. [Stillwater's Universal library](https://github.com/stillwater-sc/universal), Peter Lindstrom's NumRep, and [SoftPosit](https://gitlab.com/cerlane/SoftPosit)). That is, this RFC does not make mention of supporting custom datatype hardware. Research into custom datatypes for machine learning has been picking up as of late; see, for example, Facebook's [Rethinking Floating Point for Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.01721) paper, and the [Deep Positron](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.01762) paper. Often, much of the initial exploration into new datatypes is done by emulating datatype hardware in software, which is slower, but allows the researcher to evaluate the numerical behavior of their datatype. TVM is perfectly primed to support this kind of exploration, and supporting software custom datatypes will take very little modification. Wi...

title: GMRES Fails Silently and Frequently from Stagnation
body_excerpt: ### Description `jax.scipy.sparse.linalg.gmres` often fails to converge when `restart` is less than the problem dimension, but will return without indicating failure. This happens in both batch and incremental mode (the below code only tests batch.) This failure (likely due to stagnation) seems to depend on the absolute difference between the problem dimension and the Krylov subspace dimension (`restart`.) ie. roughly 90% of the time GMRES will fail silently on a problem of dimension 25 if `restart` = 20, and will still fail 90% of the time with a problem of dimension 100 and `restart` = 95. The failure rate jumps as high as 30% with even a 1 dimensional difference between the problem and Krylov subspace. In addition to the dangerous silent failure, this has some major implications for the implementation of the algorithm as a whole. It implies 30% of the time an incremental solve with `restart >= problem dim` may require computing the Kyrlov subpsace all the way to `problem_dim`, and 90% of the time to within 5 dimensions of it. title: jnp.linalg.norm() underflows
body_excerpt: Simple example: ``` jnp.linalg.norm(jnp.array([1e-20], jnp.float32)) ``` produces 0. Denormals are flushed to zero, and 1e-20**2 is smaller than the smallest normal float32. It's possible to define a non-underflowing Euclidean norm using variadic reductions: ``` def norm2(xs): def reducer(xs, ys): (ssq_x, scale_x) = xs (ssq_y, scale_y) = ys scale = lax.max(scale_x, scale_y) scale_is_zero = lax.eq(scale, jnp.float32(0)) ssq = ssq_x * (scale_x/scale)** 2 + ssq_y * (scale_y / scale)**2 return (lax.select(scale_is_zero, jnp.ones_like(ssq), ssq), scale) ssq_y, scale_y = lax.reduce( (np.ones_like(x), jnp.abs(x)), (jnp.float32(1), jnp.float32(0)), reducer, dimensions=(0,)) return scale_y * jnp.sqrt(ssq_y) ``` We should determine whether we want to do this; if so it probably needs to be implemented as a primitive. Interestingly `numpy.linalg.norm` also produces 0 if the CPU `ftz` flag is set (e.g., via the `daz` package), but `scipy.linalg.norm` does not.

body_excerpt: cuML uses dmlc/treelite to implement FIL and tree serialization. Treelite currently has many outstanding issues: * Model serialization is slow (https://github.com/dmlc/treelite/issues/156) * LightGBM and sklearn models require float64, but Treelite uses float32 (dmlc/treelite#77 dmlc/treelite#94 dmlc/treelite#155) * Treelite doesn't support majority voting for multi-class classifiers (dmlc/treelite#149) * cuML uses Conda to set up prerequisites and dependencies. Treelite is a lone exception and not available on Conda. * The Treelite package on PyPI is very outdated. * CMake build and setup.py in Treelite is quite complex and broken in some places. title: [BUG] Reduce memory footprint of mnmg kmeans
body_excerpt: This issue has two parts: 1. Currently our mnmg kmeans implementation performs a copy of the input partitions in order to concatenate the partitions on each workers into a single partition. This doubles the memory usage of the algorithm and severely limits the scale. This simplified the logic of the mnmg implementation when we first introduced cuml's mnmg capabilities but now that we've built several other mnmg algorithms, the additional overhead is no longer jusifiable and this should be fixed. title: Support incremental autotuning
body_excerpt: It would be possible to take an "incremental" approach to autotuning as an alternative to the existing exhaustive approach. That is instead of trying all config variants on each unique param-set attempt, **a single config is attempted and timings stored** and the fn returns. This means over the course of many runs (of the same param-set) eventually all config variants will be benched. After this many runs there should be some best config to use from then after. This approach has some advantages: * Initial performance is not significantly affected, it will only be as slow as the slowest config and never incur full tuning slowdown. This is particularly useful for fn calls with param-sets that are rarely or uniquely used, full tuning would not be worth it. * The lack of initial slowdowns may allow this to be used by default in more places improving performance for many people as they run fns over time. Disadvantages: * Before all config variants have been benched performance will vary. Some logging of the increment tuning state should help convey to users why this is the case. * It takes longer to tune everything. title: [Tracking Issue][TFLite] Support quantized operator import in Relax frontend
body_excerpt: ## Problem The Relax TFLite frontend currently has two related blockers for quantized TFLite import. First, quantized tensors are blocked early in `get_tensors()` by the tensor quantization metadata guard. After preserving tensor-level quantization metadata (`scale`, `zero_point`, and `axis`) and allowing the frontend to proceed further, the next blocker appears at the operator conversion stage: ```text NameError: name '_qnn' is not defined ``` This happens because the frontend contains quantized operator conversion paths that reference non-existent `_qnn.op.*` APIs. At the same time, Relax already provides `quantize` / `dequantize` operators with C++ registration, Python APIs, legalization to TE, and tests. This suggests that quantized TFLite operators may initially be imported using QDQ decomposition around existing Relax ops, rather than requiring a new set of fused QNN operators as the first step. This issue tracks the work needed to support quantized TFLite operator import in the Relax frontend. ## Affected `_qnn.op.*` calls The TFLite frontend (`python/tvm/relax/frontend/tflite/tflite_frontend.py`) references 7 non-existent QNN ops across 18 call sites: | Op | Call sites |...

title: Cleanup warnings in test suite

title: add `is_tracer`, `assert_concrete` functions to API
body_excerpt: I find that I sometimes want to make sure a jitting fails early when being `jit`ted with a tracer where the function requires a concrete value, rather than giving a lengthy stack trace that obfuscates what went wrong. For this, I am using the following methods and thought it might be convenient and instructive to have them be part of the JAX API: ```python def is_tracer(obj: Any) -> bool: return isinstance(obj, jax.core.Tracer) def assert_concrete(obj: Any, obj_name: str = ""): if is_tracer(obj): if not obj_name: obj_name = "<Unnamed>" _msg = f"Object `{obj_name}` needs to be concrete, but was a Tracer. " raise ConcretizationTypeError(obj, _msg) ``` I then use these at the beginning of a function: ```python def test_function(array, concrete_num): assert_concrete(concrete_num, "concrete_num") slicer = min(5, concrete_num) return array[slicer:] ```

title: [FEA] Support for HDBSCAN relative_validity
body_excerpt: The CPU hdbscan [library provides](https://github.com/scikit-learn-contrib/hdbscan/blob/c5fcf4b3829d391eadd14598736a763952790a82/hdbscan/hdbscan_.py#L1457) a `relative_validity_` attribute, which is a "[fast approximation of the Density Based Cluster Validity (DBCV) score](https://hdbscan.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api.html#id92)". It would be nice to support this in cuML, even if we ran this on CPU (it's _fairly_ lightweight) ```python from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs import cuml import hdbscan # !pip install hdbscan N = 1000 K = 10 X, y = make_blobs( n_samples=N, n_features=K, random_state=12 ) clusterer = hdbscan.HDBSCAN(gen_min_span_tree=True) clusterer.fit(X) print(clusterer.relative_validity_) 0.8025289855360727 ``` Similar to https://github.com/rapidsai/cuml/issues/4497

title: [BUG] Missing dual_gap_ attribute in Lasso/ElasticNet implementation
body_excerpt: ## Problem Two scikit-learn tests are failing in cuML's Lasso implementation: - `test_lasso_zero` - `test_lasso_toy` The failures occur because these tests check for the `dual_gap_` attribute, which is present in scikit-learn's implementation but missing in cuML's. ## Impact - Test failures in scikit-learn compatibility tests - Missing functionality that could be useful for users who rely on this metric ## Additional Context - cuML uses different solvers (CD and QN) than scikit-learn - The duality gap computation may not be feasible or meaningful with cuML's solver implementations - This is a scikit-learn specific implementation detail that may not align with cuML's optimization approach
